summary: One spelling with two uses in scripture. לֶחֶם is bread and, beyond it, food of every kind and a meal (an angel refuses Manoah’s “bread”, a kid, Jdg 13:15–16), the offerings as Yahweh’s bread, the bread set before him, and the manna “bread from heaven”; the qal verb is “eat”. The niphal לָחַם is “fight”, and מִלְחָמָה, the commonest of the root’s words after לֶחֶם, is battle and war, as in Num 10:9, where Israel blows the trumpets when they go to war and is remembered before Yahweh. Arabic, with the same ḥ, has laḥm “flesh”, laḥama “knit together”, iltaḥama and talāḥama “clash in close combat”, and malḥama both “butcher’s place” and “bloody battle”, so the cognates put both uses under one older root, though how food and fighting join is not shown by the evidence.

senses.definition: Bread baked from grain, eaten by the piece or carried as loaves: the staple food set beside water and wine.

evidence.note: When Yahweh breaks the staff of לֶחֶם, ten women bake your לֶחֶם in one oven and give it back by weight.
Jesse sends David with roasted grain and “ten loaves of this לֶחֶם”.
Abraham offers “a morsel (פַּת) of לֶחֶם”; Sarah bakes cakes of fine flour (v. 6).
Melchizedek brings out לֶחֶם and wine.
Abraham gives Hagar לֶחֶם and a skin of water.
The ravens bring Elijah לֶחֶם and flesh morning and evening.
A loaf of לֶחֶם daily from the bakers’ street, until all the לֶחֶם in the city was gone.
Children ask for לֶחֶם, and no one breaks it for them.
“Send your לֶחֶם on the face of the waters.”

senses.definition: Food in general, flesh included, and “to eat לֶחֶם” is to take a meal; the food by which man and beast live, and so a man’s living or allowance.

evidence.note: Manoah offers to prepare a kid; the angel answers, “I will not eat of your לֶחֶם.”
“In the sweat of your face you shall eat לֶחֶם until you return to the ground.”
Famine in all lands, “but in all the land of Egypt there was לֶחֶם”; the grain sold in Gen 41:55–57 and 47:13–19.
Jacob calls his brothers “to eat לֶחֶם”, a meal after the sacrifice.
Joseph: “Set on לֶחֶם”, the meal at noon (v. 25, 32).
“Call him, that he may eat לֶחֶם.”
David ends his fast: they set לֶחֶם before him and he ate.
He makes grass grow for the cattle and plants for man, “to bring forth לֶחֶם from the earth”, and לֶחֶם sustains man’s heart (v. 15).
He gives לֶחֶם to all flesh.
He gives the beast its לֶחֶם, and the young ravens.
The ant prepares her לֶחֶם in summer.
“The earth, out of it comes לֶחֶם.”
Jacob asks for לֶחֶם to eat and clothing to wear.
He who tills his ground will be satisfied with לֶחֶם.
Nehemiah and his brothers did not eat “the לֶחֶם of the governor”, the governor’s allowance levied on the people (v. 15, 18).
Mephibosheth will eat לֶחֶם at David’s table always: his keep.
To share your לֶחֶם with the hungry.

senses.definition: The grain bread is made from, and the yield of the land.

evidence.note: “לֶחֶם is crushed”, but not threshed for ever: bread grain.
Rain for the seed, and “לֶחֶם, the produce of the ground”.
When you eat of the לֶחֶם of the land, you lift up a heave offering.

senses.definition: Once, a tree’s fruit, its “food”.

evidence.note: “Let us destroy the tree with its לֶחֶם, and cut him off from the land of the living.”

senses.definition: The offerings made by fire, fat and flesh included, called the bread, the food, of Israel’s God, offered by the priests at his table, the altar.

evidence.note: The priests offer “the fire offerings of Yahweh, the לֶחֶם of their God”, and so must be holy.
“My offering, my לֶחֶם for my fire offerings, a soothing scent to me, you shall keep to offer to me in its appointed time.”
The fat of the peace offering burned on the altar is “לֶחֶם of a fire offering to Yahweh”.
No priest with a blemish may come near to offer the לֶחֶם of his God (also v. 21–22).
Foreigners brought into the sanctuary “when you offer my לֶחֶם, the fat and the blood”.
“You offer defiled לֶחֶם on my altar … in that you say, The table of Yahweh is contemptible.”

senses.definition: Bread set before Yahweh or eaten in the holy place: the bread of the presence on the table, the bread of the ordination, the leavened bread of the thank offering, and the two loaves of firstfruits of Lev 23.

evidence.note: “You shall set לֶחֶם פָּנִים on the table before me continually.”
“The continual לֶחֶם shall be on it.”
Frankincense on the rows “for the לֶחֶם, as a memorial, a fire offering to Yahweh”; the twelve cakes set out every sabbath and eaten by Aaron and his sons in a holy place (vv. 5–9).
The priest gives David holy bread, “for there was no לֶחֶם there but the לֶחֶם הַפָּנִים, taken from before Yahweh”.
Kohathites over “the לֶחֶם of the row”, to prepare it every sabbath.
Aaron and his sons eat the ram’s flesh and “the לֶחֶם in the basket” of the ordination.
With the thank offering, cakes of leavened לֶחֶם.
At the feast of weeks: “Out of your dwellings you shall bring two wave loaves (לֶחֶם תְּנוּפָה) … baked with leaven, firstfruits to Yahweh.”
With the לֶחֶם, seven lambs, a bull and two rams.
The priest waves the two lambs “with the לֶחֶם of the firstfruits”, holy to Yahweh for the priest.
No לֶחֶם, parched grain or fresh grain eaten until the day the sheaf of firstfruits is brought.
The clean priest eats of the holy things, “for it is his לֶחֶם”.

senses.definition: The manna Yahweh rained on Israel in the wilderness, named bread from heaven, given so that Israel would know that man lives by what comes from Yahweh’s mouth.

evidence.note: “Behold, I will rain לֶחֶם from heaven for you.”
Moses: “It is the לֶחֶם which Yahweh has given you to eat.”
An omer kept, that the generations may see the לֶחֶם he fed them with.
He fed you with manna, “to make you know that man does not live by לֶחֶם alone, but man lives by every word that goes out of the mouth of Yahweh”.
“Man ate the לֶחֶם of the mighty”, the grain of heaven of v. 24.
He satisfied them with the לֶחֶם of heaven.
The crowd quotes the manna as “bread from heaven”.
“Moses did not give you the bread from heaven, but my Father gives you the true bread from heaven.”

senses.definition: What fills a life as bread fills a man: tears, ashes, sorrow, wickedness, falsehood; wisdom’s bread; and enemies who are “our bread”, to be eaten up.

evidence.note: “You have fed them with the לֶחֶם of tears.”
“My tears have been my לֶחֶם day and night.”
“I have eaten ashes like לֶחֶם.”
To eat the לֶחֶם of toil.
“They eat the לֶחֶם of wickedness and drink the wine of violence.”
לֶחֶם of falsehood is sweet to a man, but afterward his mouth is filled with gravel.
She does not eat the לֶחֶם of idleness.
Wisdom calls: “Come, eat of my לֶחֶם and drink of the wine I have mixed.”
“Why do you spend money for what is not לֶחֶם?” Hear, and your soul shall live (v. 3).
“Not a famine of לֶחֶם, nor a thirst for water, but of hearing the words of Yahweh.”
Joshua and Caleb: “Do not fear the people of the land, for they are our לֶחֶם; their shade has gone from them.”
The unleavened bread is “לֶחֶם of affliction”, for in haste Israel came out of Egypt.

evidence.locator: לֶחֶם → ἄρτος ×229 (lemma count, MACULA alignment); Lev.23.14, Lev.23.17, Lev.23.20, Exo.16.4, Exo.25.30, Deu.8.3, Psa.41.10

evidence.note: Quoting Deu 8:3: “Man shall not live by ἄρτος alone, but by every word that goes out through the mouth of God.”
The manna of Exo 16:4 and Psa 78:24 as “the bread from heaven”; “I am the ἄρτος of life” (v. 35).
“The ἄρτος that I will give is my flesh, for the life of the world.”
Quoting Psa 41:10: “He who eats ἄρτος with me has lifted up his heel against me.”
David ate “the ἄρτους of the presentation”, the bread of the presence of 1Sa 21:7.
In the first tabernacle, the table and the setting out of the ἄρτων.
From Isa 55:10: he who gives seed to the sower and ἄρτον for food.

parallels.note: Bread and water, the bare needs of life, given or taken away.

evidence.note: “He will bless your לֶחֶם and your water.”
Yahweh removes all supply of לֶחֶם and all supply of water.

parallels.note: Bread and wine, the meal and the feast.

evidence.note: “Eat your לֶחֶם with joy and drink your wine with a merry heart.”

parallels.note: Food and clothing, what a man needs to live.

evidence.note: He loves the stranger, giving him לֶחֶם and clothing.
He called a famine on the land and broke every staff of לֶחֶם.

phrases.gloss: bread of the presence, set before Yahweh
bread of waving, the two wave loaves of the feast of weeks
staff of bread: the supply that holds life up
bread of the mighty: the manna

senses.definition: A fight between armies on a field: joined, spread, pressed, won or lost.

evidence.note: The Philistines set themselves in array against Israel, “and the מִלְחָמָה spread, and Israel was struck”.
The army going out to the battle line, shouting for the מִלְחָמָה.
“The מִלְחָמָה was scattered over the face of all the land, and the forest devoured more people than the sword.”
The מִלְחָמָה went up that day, and the king was propped up in his chariot.
The king of Moab saw that the מִלְחָמָה was too strong for him.
Joshua hears the people shout: “There is a noise of מִלְחָמָה in the camp.”
“Why have you come out to set the מִלְחָמָה in array?”

senses.definition: A state of war between peoples or houses, lasting for days or years, the opposite of peace; and warfare as a craft that is learned and taught.

evidence.note: “A time of מִלְחָמָה and a time of שָׁלוֹם.”

“When you go to מִלְחָמָה in your land against the adversary who oppresses you, you shall sound an alarm with the trumpets, and you will be remembered before Yahweh your God and saved from your enemies.”
The four kings made מִלְחָמָה with the kings of Sodom and Gomorrah.
“There was long מִלְחָמָה between the house of Saul and the house of David.”
מִלְחָמָה between Rehoboam and Jeroboam all their days.
God did not lead them by the Philistines’ road, lest the people see מִלְחָמָה and turn back to Egypt.
“When you go out to מִלְחָמָה against your enemies … do not be afraid of them.”
The nations were left “to teach them מִלְחָמָה”, those who had not known it.
“Who teaches my hands for the battle and my fingers for מִלְחָמָה.”
“I am for peace, but when I speak, they are for מִלְחָמָה.”
“Nation shall not lift up sword against nation, nor shall they learn מִלְחָמָה any more.”
He makes מִלְחָמוֹת cease to the end of the earth.
“Bow and sword and מִלְחָמָה I will break from the land, and make them lie down safely.”
With good counsel make מִלְחָמָה.

senses.definition: War that belongs to Yahweh: he is a man of war, mighty in battle; the battle is his, and Israel’s wars are fought as his.

evidence.note: “Yahweh is a man of מִלְחָמָה; Yahweh is his name.”
“Yahweh does not save with sword and spear, for the מִלְחָמָה is Yahweh’s, and he will give you into our hand.”
“The מִלְחָמָה is not yours but God’s.”
“Yahweh strong and mighty, Yahweh mighty in מִלְחָמָה.”
“Yahweh has מִלְחָמָה with Amalek from generation to generation.”
“The book of the מִלְחֲמֹת of Yahweh.”
Saul to David: “Fight the מִלְחֲמוֹת of Yahweh.”
Yahweh goes out like a mighty man, like a man of מִלְחָמוֹת he stirs up zeal.
The horse is prepared for the day of מִלְחָמָה, but salvation is Yahweh’s.

evidence.locator: מִלְחָמָה → πόλεμος ×206 (lemma count, MACULA alignment); Num.10.9 → πόλεμον; Exo.15.3 → πολέμους

evidence.note: “If the trumpet gives an uncertain sound, who will prepare himself for πόλεμον?”, the trumpet that called Israel to war (Num 10:9).
The beast and the kings of the earth gathered to make πόλεμον against him who sits on the horse.
“Where do πόλεμοι and fightings among you come from? Is it not from your desires?”

parallels.note: War beside the sword that wages it.

evidence.note: “I will not save them by bow or by sword or by מִלְחָמָה.”
Your men shall fall by the sword, and your mighty in the מִלְחָמָה.
In famine he redeems you from death, and in מִלְחָמָה from the power of the sword.
Prophets who cry “Peace” while they have something to eat, and prepare מִלְחָמָה against him who puts nothing in their mouths.
David may not build the house, “for you are a man of מִלְחָמוֹת and have shed blood”.

phrases.gloss: the men of war, the fighting men

evidence.note: “How the mighty have fallen, and the weapons of מִלְחָמָה perished!”

senses.definition: To fight with an enemy, people against people or man against man; with בְּ, עִם or אֶת of the enemy, with עַל of a city besieged, and with לְ of the one fought for.

evidence.note: “Amalek came and fought (וַיִּלָּחֶם) with Israel in Rephidim”; Joshua is sent to fight him (v. 9–10).
David: “Your servant will go and fight with this Philistine.”
Goliath: “If he is able to fight with me and kill me …”
Lest when מִלְחָמָה comes, Israel joins the enemy and fights against us.
The five kings encamp against Gibeon and fight against it.
When you come near a city to fight against it, proclaim peace to it.
“Did Balak ever strive with Israel, or did he ever fight (נִלְחֹם נִלְחַם) against them?”
“Fight for (עַל) your master’s house.”
“Fight for your brothers, your sons and your daughters, your wives and your houses.”
“From heaven the stars fought; from their courses they fought against Sisera.”
“They surrounded me with words of hatred and fought against me without cause”: fighting with words.

senses.gloss: Yahweh fights (for his people, or against them)
senses.definition: Yahweh himself fights: for Israel against their enemies, so that they need only stand still, or against his people when they rebel, or against the nations at his coming.

evidence.note: “Yahweh will fight for you, and you shall be silent.”
Egypt: “Let us flee from Israel, for Yahweh fights for them.”
“Yahweh your God is he who goes with you, to fight for you against your enemies, to save you.”
No day like it, “for Yahweh fought for Israel”.
One man of you chases a thousand, for Yahweh fights for you.
“Our God will fight for us.”
“You will not need to fight in this; stand still and see the salvation of Yahweh.”
“With him is an arm of flesh, but with us is Yahweh our God, to help us and to fight our battles (מִלְחֲמֹתֵנוּ).”
Abijah: God is with us at our head, and his priests with the trumpets; “do not fight against Yahweh.”
They rebelled and grieved his holy spirit, “so he turned to be their enemy; he himself fought against them”.
“I myself will fight against you with an outstretched hand.”
“Yahweh will go out and fight against those nations, as when he fights on a day of battle”, his feet standing on the Mount of Olives (v. 4).
To Jeremiah: “They will fight against you, but they will not prevail against you, for I am with you.”

senses.definition: To eat, used in Proverbs and Psalms with לֶחֶם or with food as its object; the passive participle is “consumed”.

evidence.note: “They eat (לָחֲמוּ) the לֶחֶם of wickedness, and drink the wine of violence.”
Wisdom: “Come, eat (לַחֲמוּ) of my לֶחֶם, and drink of the wine I have mixed.”
“When you sit to eat (לִלְחוֹם) with a ruler, consider well what is before you.”
“Do not eat the לֶחֶם of one with an evil eye.”
“Let me not eat (אֶלְחַם) of their delicacies.”
“Wasted by hunger and consumed (לְחֻמֵי) by burning heat”: the passive participle, set beside hunger.

senses.definition: In three Psalms, to fight against someone; the active participle is “one who fights”, the enemy.

evidence.note: “Contend, Yahweh, with those who contend with me; fight (לְחַם) those who fight me (לֹחֲמָי)”, beside רִיב, “strive”.
“All the day one fighting (לֹחֵם) oppresses me.”
“Many fight (לֹחֲמִים) against me.”

evidence.locator: לָחַם → πολεμέω ×34 (lemma count, MACULA alignment), and inflected forms besides; Exo.14.14 יִלָּחֵם → πολεμήσει; Psa.35.1 לְחַם → πολέμησον

evidence.note: He who sits on the white horse “in righteousness judges and makes war (πολεμεῖ)”.
“These will make war with the Lamb, and the Lamb will overcome them.”
“I will fight against them with the sword of my mouth.”

parallels.note: To strive, contend, beside to fight.

words.summary: Once, in Deborah’s song, of the fighting that came to Israel’s gates when they chose new gods. The word is read from the verb “fight” and its sense is fixed only by the context of Jdg 5:8; the construction is unclear.

senses.definition: War come to the cities: when Israel chose new gods, there was fighting at the gates, and not a shield or spear was seen among forty thousand.

evidence.note: “They chose new gods; then לָחֶם שְׁעָרִים”, fighting at the gates, with no shield or spear in Israel.

words.summary: Twice, in poetry. In Zephaniah it stands beside “blood” for what is poured out of the slain, so the flesh or bowels; in Job it is read either as the wicked man’s food or his flesh. Arabic laḥm “flesh” is the closest cognate.

senses.definition: The flesh of the slain, set beside their blood.

evidence.note: “Their blood shall be poured out like dust, and their לְחוּם like dung.”
When he is about to fill his belly, God sends his burning anger on him “and rains it upon him בִּלְחוּמוֹ”, in his eating, or on his flesh.

words.summary: Biblical Aramaic, once: the meal, the food, made into a great feast.

senses.definition: A great meal given by a king to his lords, with wine.

evidence.note: “Belshazzar the king made a great לְחֶם for a thousand of his lords, and drank wine before the thousand.”

words.gloss: bread, loaf; the bread of life
words.summary: The Peshitta’s word for bread, where the Greek has ἄρτος: Deu 8:3 quoted, the bread of the presence, the bread from heaven, and the bread of the Lord’s supper.

senses.definition: Bread and food, as the Hebrew לֶחֶם, quoted from Deu 8:3 and asked for daily.

evidence.note: “Not by לַחְמָא alone does a man live, but by every word that goes out from the mouth of God”: Deu 8:3.
“Give us the לַחְמָא of our need today.”
David ate the bread of the table of Yahweh, as 1Sa 21:7.

senses.gloss: the bread from heaven, the bread of life
senses.definition: Jesus names himself the bread from heaven that the manna stood for, and the bread broken at the supper his body.

evidence.note: Not Moses but “my Father gives you the true לַחְמָא from heaven”.
“I am the לַחְמָא of life.”
The night he was betrayed he took לַחְמָא, gave thanks, broke it and said, “This is my body.”
“We, being many, are one לַחְמָא, one body.”

words.summary: The Peshitta’s verb of this root is not “eat” or “fight” but hostility and threats. Its tie to the Hebrew “fight” is likely, through hostility shown in words (compare Psa 109:3), but no cognate shows it, so the link is not clear.

senses.definition: Passive participle: set against someone, bearing a grudge.

evidence.note: Herodias “was hostile (לְחִימָא) to him and wanted to kill him”.

senses.definition: To threaten, with words meant to frighten someone off.

evidence.note: “Let us threaten them not to speak again in this name.”
“When he suffered, he did not threaten, but committed his judgement to the judge of righteousness.”

words.summary: The Peshitta’s noun “threat”, from the verb לְחַם “threaten”; its tie to the Hebrew root’s senses is as unclear as the verb’s.

senses.definition: Words of menace against someone.

evidence.note: “Lord, look upon their threats, and give your servants to speak your word openly.”
Saul, still full of threats and murder against the disciples.

cognates.note: Arabic’s common word for flesh and meat; Lane’s supplement has “dates having flesh” (tamr lahu laḥm) and laḥḥām “a butcher”. Where Hebrew and Aramaic have “bread, food”, Arabic has “meat”: each the staple food. Hebrew לֶחֶם itself covers a kid served as a meal (Jdg 13:15–16), and לְחוּם is “flesh” (Zep 1:17). Arabic ḥ (ح), not ḫ (خ), stands behind ח.

cognates.gloss: knit together, close up; be closely joined; (of armies) clash, fight at close quarters
cognates.note: Lane’s supplement gives form IV “closed up the hole with a patch”, “the consolidating of wounds”, form VI talāḥama “it was joined, or knit, together” and form VIII iltaḥama “it coalesced, consolidated, closed up, or became closely united”. Wiktionary adds for talāḥama and iltaḥama “to clash, to fight, to engage in close combat”. Fighting as armies closing with each other answers to the Hebrew niphal “fight”, which is itself reciprocal in form. Same ḥ as laḥm “flesh”.

evidence.locator: Arabic, تلاحم (talāḥama), verb: “to clash, to fight, to engage in close combat”; التحم (iltaḥama), verb: “to clash, to come to blows”

cognates.gloss: bloody battle, slaughter; also a place of flesh, a butcher’s shop
cognates.note: The same pattern as Hebrew מִלְחָמָה (m- prefix, -a ending). Wiktionary gives both “a place where meat is stored or sold” and “bloody battle, slaughter”; Lane’s supplement has the plural malāḥim, sing. malḥama, “a place of much flesh”. The one Arabic word joins the flesh and the battle.

evidence.locator: Arabic, ملحمة (malḥama), noun: “bloody battle, slaughter, massacre, bloodbath”; cognate with Hebrew מִלְחָמָה and Phoenician mlḥmt

cognates.gloss: (verb) eat; (causative) feed; (noun) food, bread, probably meat
cognates.note: Segert’s glossary gives the G stem “to eat” (KTU 1.4 IV 35), the Š stem “to feed”, and the noun lḥm “food, bread”, in KTU 1.114:7 probably “meat”. Ugaritic writes ḥ (𐎈) and ḫ (𐎃) apart, and has ḥ here.
The same noun as Hebrew מִלְחָמָה, with the same ḥ. Not in Segert’s selected glossary; Segert’s page was not found for it.

Phoenician qal “fight”: Kilamuwa’s house was among more powerful kings, “each of whom stretched forth his hand to fight” (KAI 24.5–6). Krahmalkov lists separately L-Ḥ-M II “join, fit (boards)” with MLḤM “joiner, carpenter”, the sense of Arabic laḥama.

evidence.locator: pp. 253–254, L-Ḥ-M I, v. qal FIGHT; KAI 24.5/6

cognates.note: In the Kition inscription, “when our enemies … came to do battle (l‘gd ‘m mlḥmt) with us”, and in Byblos 13.5.

evidence.locator: p. 283, MLḤMT, n.f. WAR, BATTLE; Kition lines 1/3; Byb. 13.5

cognates.note: Moabite, on the Mesha stele: “and I fought (ואלתחם) against the city and took it” (line 11), “and I fought against it from the break of dawn until noon” (line 15), the king of Israel dwelling in Jahaz “when he fought against me (בהלתחמה בי)” (line 19), and Kemosh’s command “go down, fight (הלתחם) against Horonaim” (line 32): the reflexive t-stem where Hebrew has the niphal.

cognates.gloss: bread, food; a meal; (once reported) meat
cognates.note: Jewish Aramaic, in the Targum of Melchizedek’s bread (Targ. Gen 14:18) and of Joseph’s “set on bread” (Targ. Gen 43:31), and “let us go and eat bread”, dine. A midrash on Zep 1:17 says that “in Arabia they call meat laḥma”. Aramaic ח does not show whether ḥ or ḫ stands behind it.

evidence.note: 1) bread: Targ. Gen. XIV, 18; XLIII, 31; Ber. 42b. 2) meat, flesh: Ex. R. s. 42, on Zeph. I, 17.

cognates.note: Akkadian lêmu (Neo-Assyrian ilemmu, ilêm) “eat, consume”. Akkadian loses ḥ but keeps ḫ, so a lêmu from *lḥm would show ḥ, as the other cognates do; recorded as possible because the derivation is argued, not shown, and Akkadian’s ordinary verb “eat” is akālu.

Krahmalkov’s L-Ḥ-M II, piel or yiphil, with MLḤM “joiner, carpenter” (RES 1319) and a Punic medical text, “close up the wound” (KAI 76 B 3, translation problematic). It matches Arabic laḥama “knit together, close up”; no word of scripture has this sense, so it is named on none.

evidence.locator: p. 254, L-Ḥ-M II; p. 283, MLḤM, n.m. JOINER

doctrine.statement: Yahweh rained לֶחֶם from heaven on Israel in the wilderness (Exo 16:4, 15) and fed them with it to humble them and “to make you know that man does not live by לֶחֶם alone, but by every word that goes out of the mouth of Yahweh” (Deu 8:3); Jesus answers with that verse when he is hungry in the wilderness (Mat 4:4). Amos foretells a famine “not of לֶחֶם … but of hearing the words of Yahweh” (Amo 8:11), and Wisdom calls men to eat her לֶחֶם (Pro 9:5; compare Isa 55:2–3). Jesus says that Moses did not give the bread from heaven, but his Father gives the true bread from heaven, that he is the bread of life, and that the bread he gives is his flesh, for the life of the world (Jhn 6:31–35, 48–51). From the verses: the manna was bread given to teach that life comes from God’s word; that word is given in his Son, and the life the bread stood for is had by receiving him, whose flesh was given for the world.

The offerings burned on the altar are called “the לֶחֶם of their God” and “my לֶחֶם” (Lev 21:6; Num 28:2), the altar “the table of Yahweh” (Mal 1:7), and twelve loaves were set on the table before him continually, every sabbath, for a memorial, then eaten by the priests in the holy place (Exo 25:30; Lev 24:5–9). At the feast of weeks Israel brought from their dwellings two loaves baked with leaven as firstfruits to Yahweh (Lev 23:17, 20). Jesus cites David’s eating of the holy bread (1Sa 21:7; Mat 12:3–4). On the night he was betrayed he took bread, broke it and said, “This is my body”, to be eaten in remembrance of him (1Co 11:23–26), and Paul writes that “we, being many, are one bread, one body, for we all partake of the one bread” (1Co 10:16–17). From the verses: what was set before Yahweh and shared at his table under the law answers to the bread of the memorial, where the many who eat it are made one body in Christ.

Yahweh is “a man of מִלְחָמָה” (Exo 15:3). At the Red Sea Israel was told, “Yahweh will fight for you, and you shall be silent” (Exo 14:14); the priest was to tell the army that Yahweh goes with them to fight for them, to save them (Deu 20:4); and when Israel went to war against an oppressor in their land, the trumpets were blown and they were remembered before Yahweh and saved from their enemies (Num 10:9). David went out to Goliath because “the battle is Yahweh’s” and he does not save by sword and spear (1Sa 17:47); Jehoshaphat was told, “You will not need to fight in this; stand still and see the salvation of Yahweh” (2Ch 20:15, 17). But when Israel rebelled, “he turned to be their enemy; he himself fought against them” (Isa 63:10), and against Jerusalem by Babylon’s hand (Jer 21:5). Zechariah sees all nations gathered against Jerusalem, and Yahweh going out to fight against them, his feet standing on the Mount of Olives (Zec 14:2–4), and John sees him who is Faithful and True, who “in righteousness judges and makes war” against the beast and the kings of the earth (Rev 19:11, 19). From the verses: Israel’s wars were Yahweh’s, won by his fighting and not their weapons, and lost when he fought against them; the last war at Jerusalem is fought by Yahweh in the one he sends at his coming.

Isaiah and Micah see the mountain of Yahweh’s house established in the last days, the law going out from Zion, and Yahweh judging among the nations: “they shall beat their swords into ploughshares … nation shall not lift up sword against nation, nor shall they learn מִלְחָמָה any more” (Isa 2:2–4; Mic 4:1–3). Hosea foretells that Yahweh will break bow, sword and מִלְחָמָה from the land and make Israel lie down safely (Hos 2:20); the psalmist sees him making wars cease to the end of the earth (Psa 46:10); and Zechariah’s king, coming to Jerusalem on an ass, cuts off the battle bow and speaks peace to the nations, his rule reaching to the ends of the earth (Zec 9:9–10). From the verses: war is ended not by men’s treaties but by Yahweh’s judgement among the nations from Zion, under his king; until then the time of war and the time of peace alternate (Ecc 3:8).

note: Drafted 2026-11-13. Root key לחמ as the database keys it. BDB keys: the database fills l.bh.aa (fight) and l.bi.aa (eat) with the same 177 tokens, so the one verb (qal eat and fight; niphal fight) names l.bh.aa only, and l.bi.aa is left unclaimed. l.bh.ab (Jdg 5:8 לָחֶם) shares its surface with every pausal לָחֶם “bread”, so its count (59) is inflated: only Jdg 5:8 is the word. Left out: the person לַחְמִי Lahmi (l.bi.ac, 1Ch 20:5; its 9 tokens also catch “my bread”), the places בֵּית לֶחֶם Bethlehem (b.bp.az) and לַחְמָס Lahmas (l.bi.ad, Jos 15:40), and the person יָשֻׁבִי לֶחֶם (1Ch 4:22): the task allowed no name entries for this root, and places cannot be name entries. m.cb.ag (מִלְחָמָה, “see לחם”) is a cross-reference with no tokens and is not claimed. Isa 47:14 לַחְמָם (root חמם) and Job 30:4 לַחְמָם (filed as qal) are counted under the noun as the brief has them. Open questions: (1) Whether “food” and “fight” are one older root: Arabic, Ugaritic and (if lêmu belongs) Akkadian all show ḥ for both, and Arabic malḥama is both “meat place” and “bloody battle”, laḥama “knit together” and iltaḥama “clash”; the entry keeps one root and says the connection is not shown. (2) The Peshitta verb לְחַם “threaten” and noun לוּחָמָא “threat” have no cognate of their own, so lexicon-support counts the root’s cognates against them. (3) Job 20:23 בִּלְחוּמוֹ “in his eating” or “on his flesh”. (4) Doctrine “yahweh-fights” reads Zec 14:3 and Rev 19:11 together of the return; doctrine “bread-before-yahweh” links the shewbread and Yahweh’s table to the memorial bread without reading a figure into the two leavened loaves of Lev 23:17. Leads not followed: Ge’ez laḥama “be strong” (Anderson–Moser GEZ003080) not checked in Dillmann or Leslau; Payne Smith not checked for Syriac ܠܚܡ; Ugaritic lḥm “fight” (Anderson–Moser UGC002482) not found in Segert.
